A range partition's hot tail isn't caused by a bad key choice in the usual sense — any monotonically increasing key (order IDs, timestamps, auto-increment) produces it, because the newest key is, by definition, always the largest one.

Splitting a range once it grows too large doesn't fix the hot tail — it just creates a new, smaller tail range that inherits the identical problem, which is why 'add capacity' alone never solves this topic's own 'Prove it' scenario.

Hash partitioning doesn't avoid the ordered-scan cost by choice — it structurally can't support it, because a hash function is specifically designed so that adjacent input keys produce unrelated outputs, which is exactly what makes the spread even.

Naive modulo hashing's fragility on resize isn't a minor inefficiency — every single key's placement formula literally contains the total node count, so changing that count changes nearly every key's answer simultaneously.

items.item: Consistent hashing and rendezvous hashing solve the identical minimal-movement problem through opposite mechanisms: one precomputes a shared ring every node agrees on, the other needs no shared state at all and recomputes the answer independently every time.

at.step: Reveal: consistent hashing and rendezvous hashing

items.item: Client-side, proxy, and coordinator routing trade the same two costs in different places: who has to know the full partition map, and how many network hops a request takes to reach the node that actually owns the data.

Partitioning and replication answer genuinely unrelated questions — a system could partition data across a thousand nodes with zero replication (one copy each), or replicate a single unpartitioned dataset across a thousand nodes (one partition, many copies); real systems do both only because both problems need solving, not because they're the same problem.

items.item: Choosing hash partitioning purely to avoid a hot tail can create a worse problem if the workload actually needs range scans — this topic's own measured range-scan cost under hash partitioning shows the opposite trade being made silently.

items.item: This topic's own executable claims use a real SHA-256-based hash function rather than Python's built-in hash() specifically because the built-in is randomized per process run by default — a reproducible, portable hash is required to make 'moves a small fraction' a stable, checkable claim.

This topic's own 'Prove it' answer generalizes: no key-space partitioning scheme, by itself, can fix a workload where every write targets the newest key — the fix has to change which partition new writes land on, which means changing the key, not the cluster size.
